utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. Douglas Stringer, Alex Demirdjian, Thomas Laugel, and Marija Bukovac for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is being brought in I've been informed that in relation to these faxes that we had in one bundle yesterday, they have been split into 14 or 15 separate entries, so they're at 65 ter 87.2 to 65 ter 87.15. So they have been divided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. So now we should give them exhibit numbers? Can we do that now or do we do that later, Mr. Registrar? Later. Okay. So the parties will be noticed about the exhibit numbers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Bosanac. I remind you that you're still under oath. Thank you. Mr. Gosnell, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: We finished yesterday discussing the removal of civilians from the hospital that was being directed by Major Sljivancanin. After that occasion, is my understanding correct that the next time you saw Mr. Sljivancanin was at around 7.00 p.m. on the 19th of November in your office with Nicolas Borsinger?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And am I right in saying that on that occasion he asked for the lists of the patients that you had in the hospital to be handed over to him? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And am I right that he insisted on taking all the copies that you had in your possession of the lists of patients in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You had wanted to keep a list yourself, but he refused that request, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And then sometime after this meeting ended, did a JNA officer come and say that he was going to take you to Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He didn't tell me exactly where he was taking me. He just said he got instructions to take me to a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: About what time was that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think around 9.00. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And then am I right that he escorted you from your office to his car and drove you to Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And yesterday we were discussing that he at least at some point was accompanied by a bearded soldier. On that occasion when he drove you to Negoslavci, this JNA officer, was he accompanied by a soldier with a long beard?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said when I was going to Negoslavci the first time around 1.00 p.m. before meeting Mile Mrksic there, the bearded soldier was in that car. He was not accompanying Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you. So when you were driven in this car to Negoslavci on the evening of the 19th, were you alone with this -- this JNA officer?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And as I understand it, you returned the next morning at around 6.00 a.m. from Negoslavci back to the hospital, and were you accompanied on that occasion by the same JNA officer?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the driver, and Marin Vidic was already in the car when I was brought there. I can't remember exactly, but that officer was not there. There was only the driver who took us back to the hospital, not Marin Vidic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, yesterday I asked you a question about the relationship between the paramilitaries and the JNA when you first saw them at the bridge, and you quite rightly asked me for a clarification, are you talking only about the bridge or are you talking more generally. So now I want to expand the question to more generally. Is it true from what you observed on the 19th and 20th of November that in your view the paramilitaries were under the control and protection of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way I saw it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did that include the White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what makes you say that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the fact that on the afternoon of the 19th the White Eagles, as they were called, wanted to get into the hospital, and the military police did not let them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was that the only reason why you came to that conclusion -- or you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also because when I was going to Negoslavci the first time, I saw that bearded member of the paramilitaries. He stopped the car to get a lift in whatever direction we were going. However, when he realised we were from the hospital, he asked us, "Are you Ustashas?" That young man who was with me, Voloder, explained that we were not Ustashas, and I saw repulsion and fury on his face. That at least was my impression because we were in the JNA vehicle. He stopped the car and got out. He did not display his fury openly towards us because he was in the JNA vehicle. He asked to get out. That's how I concluded that this man who was full of hatred and anger had some sort of respect for the JNA vehicle which was under the control of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And do you also come to the conclusion that the paramilitaries were under the control and the protection of the JNA because on various occasions you saw paramilitary soldiers together with JNA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And because you saw them being transported in JNA vehicles?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And because you saw them acquiescing to instructions by JNA officers?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, on the morning of the 20th of November, 1991, you say that there was a meeting, a staff meeting, that Major Sljivancanin instructed you to convene in the hospital. Do you remember about what time that was that the meeting convened?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you've testified that on that occasion Sljivancanin said that as of that day the hospital would be under the competence of the VMA, and you describe that as the Military Medical Academy. Is that an organ of the JNA, the Military Medical Academy?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And were there officers from the VMA already present at that meeting at 7.30 on the morning of the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: About how many were there as far as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five, I think. Four or five. I can't remember exactly any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And at any point did they take the floor and say anything during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, they were silent.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you stay to the end of the meeting or did Major Sljivancanin tell you to leave at some point before the end of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that the times when I managed the hospital are over, that I can go back to my office, and escorted by JNA officers I returned to my office. Then after, perhaps, ten minutes another soldier came and said he was taking me and Marin Vidic to a meeting, and then around 8.15 we left the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you were taken where?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the JNA barracks in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And am I right that you stayed there in the JNA barracks in Vukovar until that night?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, madam, I want to now go back to the period before the fall of Vukovar and to address a question to you about the period during the siege of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if we could please have 65 ter 04469, which is Defence tab 17. And this is transcript page 423 of the document. And it's in English only since it's a transcript, an ICTY transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, madam, I'm sorry, but we don't have a B/C/S version, so what I'm going to do is very slowly and carefully read what you said during your testimony in the Dokmanovic case, and I know this was a very long time ago, but I want to see whether or not this is still your view. And you were asked the following question: "Did you see who had civilian authority --" And before I continue reading, Dr. Bosanac, I should just inform you that this question and answer, there appears to be a little bit of a misunderstanding between you and the questioner. So please wait until you -- I get to the very end of the passage before I ask you to respond to my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, Your Honours, but why is this transcript being put to the witness? Is this for impeachment purposes or does counsel wish to lead something new? Are we moving to a new topic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm leading because I'm allowed to lead, Mr. President, and I'm using the transcript to lead the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: He's allowed to lead for his questions. There is no need to put a document before -- I mean, again, documents used on the screen can be used for impeaching or refreshing the witness's memory. I believe that the procedure should be to put the question first. Once he has an answer, he can then lead furthermore, but I think that he has to lay a foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is not true. I do not -- I am permitted to lead using whatever material I wish, and I've done this before on other cases, and there was never any objection from the Prosecution, and it was permitted by the Chambers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Overruled. Please proceed, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So, madam, here is the passage, and here was your testimony: "Q. Did you see who had civilian authority under control in Vukovar, that is while you were there? "A. The representative, the highest representative of the civilian authorities was Maric, and who was responsible for Vukovar municipality. What was happening behind the front lines held by the JNA I do not know. "Q. So you were talking about Marin Vidic who was representative of the Croatian authorities? "A. Yes. He was the representative of the Croatian authorities in Vukovar. "Q. Did you meet any representative of any Serbian authorities? Was there any Serbian authority then? "A. No, I did not. I am not aware that there was any." Now, is it correct, Dr. Bosanac, that at the time, August, September, October, and up until the fall of Vukovar on the 19th of November, that you were not aware whether there was any Serbian civilian authority on the other side of the JNA lines as you put it in your answer here?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me if I knew if there were some other authorities. No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Counsel. I apologise for intervening on this. Just to state the Prosecution's view is that what just happened actually should happen in reverse. He said: "Dr. Bosanac, at the time --" yeah, "is it correct you were not aware whether there was any Serbian civilian authority." It's our understanding that using prior statements of a witness should be linked to either refreshing recollection or impeaching so that in fact isn't what should be happening, shouldn't that last question have been put first, and then if the witness says, "Yes, that's my recollection," then that's the evidence. If the witness says, "Well, I can't remember" or "I don't remember ever saying that," then in accordance with guideline 18 of the Trial Chamber's pre-trial guidelines on refreshing recollection, the prior statement could be shown to the witness and then you say, "Well, Witness, does this refresh your recollection on this point" or "does this refresh your recollection about having had said this before," or if the witness says something that's completely contrary, then of course the transcript could used for impeachment, to say, "Well, in fact, what you're saying now is inconsistent with what you said before," but what's just occurred is the opposite. That is, the transcript is led. It's like showing a photograph to the witness, or we've had situations where a document or a photograph has been put on the screen before the witness has had a chance to comment, and it tends to then colour the testimony that follows. And it's our submission, again I apologise for intervening, that that's what's happened here. The transcript is shown. It's read into the record. It's not clear whether that's going to be a part of the record in this case, what's being read to the witness before she responds, when in fact the question should come. And then if the transcript is needed, then the appropriate time for impeachment or refreshing is then to follow up on the witness's response, but to put the question first rather than use the question to just confirm something that's been read into the record from a prior statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I may, I confess that I have a slightly different problem with the -- in that the -- without going to what Mr. Stringer has just said, the portion of the transcript was put, and I heard a question, and it struck me that I trust the witness was able to understand the -- I simply -- unless I'm missing something, I simply didn't get the question in the context of what was put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stringer, we hear what you're saying. What do you suggest, or is this meant to be an objection or a reconsideration motion or --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I hate to use the word "reconsideration." And, Your Honour, we recognise the Chamber has already ruled on this point. I guess if I could offer this as an observation of what the Prosecution views as the appropriate procedure and will continue to object when it's our position that transcripts are being used in a way that's not consistent with the Chamber's guidelines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is it also true that specifically on the 19th and the 20th of November, 1991, that you did not see any indication of the presence of civilian authorities in Vukovar? And by "civilian authorities," I mean any civilian authorities that might have existed on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th and the 20th November, I was in contact with Marin Vidic who was the government commissioner for Vukovar municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Madam --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That for me was the only civilian authority in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And is it true that in terms of your contacts on the 19th and the 20th, you only had contact with JNA officials on the Serb side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, madam, I'd like to ask you a few questions about your time at Sremska Mitrovica, if I may. And I understand that you were questioned in Sremska Mitrovica by someone who you described as Colonel or Captain Branko; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 03028, Defence tab 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is the man pictured in this photograph Colonel or Captain Branko as you knew him?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I'm not familiar with this photo. As a matter of fact, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you ever come to know Captain or Colonel Branko by any other name?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you feel while you were being questioned by Colonel Branko that you were under a certain amount of duress as to how he wished your statement to be prepared or the content of your statement?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He instructed me how to draft that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And can you tell us, if possible, or if you know, from the way in which he was instructing you how to prepare the statement what his agenda or interest was as to how the statement should appear, the content of the statement?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I realise that he wanted me to prepare a statement to the effect of what was going on in Vukovar during the aggression against the hospital and its siege. This is the way I understood the instructions. In that statement, I wanted to describe and repeat everything I had already included in my appeals, how many shells had fallen, what had happened, but he told me not to do it in the way I wanted to do it. He wanted me to include only the facts on which he questioned me, and then he told me that the time would come for me to describe things in my own words at the end of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And specifically in respect of the events of the 19th and 20th of November, did you sense that he was trying to have you present events in a particular way?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that he asked me about the number of wounded, what kinds of wounds they had sustained, and that's what I put in my statement. I don't know exactly what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, let me -- let me make it clear then. Did you sense that there were some individuals or groups whose actions he did not want to be presented in your statement in terms of the events of the 19th and 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I did not have that impression. I didn't know what was going on. All I know is that he wanted me to write where the dead were buried, and I had to draw a sketch of the graves where the dead were buried. I suggested that we should go to Vukovar there and then and that I should show him the places where we had buried our dead who were killed by shells. I remember that he told me that Vukovar was not a safe area and that we could not go there. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The reason I ask this question, Dr. Bosanac, is because I've looked at your -- the statement that you've prepared while you were at Sremska Mitrovica prison, and there's no mention of Major Sljivancanin directing the removal of civilians from the hospital on the afternoon of the 19th of November, which you've described here. Now, was that because Colonel Branko wanted you to omit that episode?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the reason is the fact that I did not finish my statement. If you look at the statement, you will see the dates. That was on a Sunday when I had still not completed my statement. I was writing it in the prison when an officer who was superior to Captain Branko arrived. He told me to collect my things because I was going to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So are you saying you didn't get the impression that he was trying to minimise the role of the JNA in these events on the 19th of November at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. I can't say whether he was trying to minimise anything. I only remember that he wanted me to write the facts, which I did. I did not finish my statement. I was interrupted. I was taken to the military prison in Belgrade, and two days later I was exchanged during an exchange of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, I'd like to go back now to the period before the outbreak of hostilities in Vukovar and the breakdown of ethnic harmony in Vukovar. Were you yourself a member of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And were members of your family members of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you know that the primary political goal of the HDZ was the independence of Croatia from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, or as it was then known, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were you yourself a supporter of independence of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you ever become concerned about any rhetoric that was being used by members of the HDZ towards Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You never felt that there was any inflammatory or provocative, threatening rhetoric used in respect of the Serbian minority in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I heard very disturbing rhetoric on the part of the Serbian Democratic Party led by Jovan Raskovic in Croatia. That's what I heard, and I was pretty shaken by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were you ever concerned about violence, acts of violence, against Serbs in Vukovar prior to the siege of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any such violent acts or behaviour, but I know what happened in Dalj and in Borovo Selo when Croatian policemen were killed as well as Croatian journalists. I know that, and those things happened before the siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You never heard that Serbian restaurants were bombed in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I heard that a restaurant in Vukovar burnt down, but not because it had been bombed. That I didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was that a Serbian restaurant?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time the restaurants there were not recognised as being either Serbian or Croatian. The restaurant had patrons of both Serbian and Croatian ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was there a kiosk of a Serbian perceived newspaper, if I can describe it like that, that was either bombed or destroyed by fire as far as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were no Serbian kiosks. At that time and today, all the kiosks sell all sorts of newspapers, both Serbian and Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you remember when Tomislav Mercep arrived in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tomislav Mercep was a resident of Vukovar. I knew him before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you remember when he was appointed to an official position?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that was in late June. That's when he became the Secretary of National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And was it understood that he was someone who promoted ethnic harmony in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tomislav Mercep was a member of the HDZ, and as I have already told you, as I have put it in my statement, in 1991 local multi-party elections took place in Vukovar. Six or seven parties ran in the elections. I don't remember how many exactly. I know that a coalition government was set up at the local level and that the president of the municipality of Vukovar, which was a local parliament, was Slavko Dokmanovic. He was --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- a member of the Reformist Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, can I please bring you back to the question, and the question was whether Tomislav Mercep was someone who promoted ethnic harmony in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is exactly what I was coming to. He was a member of the party which was legally elected and which was one of the coalition partners in the local authorities of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you ever become aware that Marin Vidic wrote an open letter about Tomislav Mercep to President Tudjman on the 18th of August, 1991?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you never heard that he had written a letter in which he says -- which apparently received some publicity, in which he said that Tomislav Mercep was not hesitating to use violent and repressive measures against the citizens of Vukovar municipality?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear that. I don't see a reason for me to comment upon things that somebody else wrote or published about the situation that I'm here to testify about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What I -- what I'm trying to ask you is whether you yourself were aware, observed, any of those violent and repressive measures that were allegedly being carried out by Tomislav Mercep according to Marin Vidic.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now during your testimony, you were shown the letter of 18th of July, 1991, in which Minister Hebrang removes Rade Popovic as the head of the Vukovar medical centre, and if I understood correctly, he was removed because he was in an unauthorised manner extending or granting leave to Serbs who were not coming to work. Is that a fair characterisation of the reasons expressed in the letter?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only Serbs. That applied to everybody who failed to present for work.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's a fair point, but isn't it true that the vast majority of the individuals who were unable and who did not come to work were those who were caught -- who were Serbs who were caught on the other side of the barricades and were not able to enter Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that period of time from the 2nd of May up until the 7th of -- 17th of July, one could go to Vukovar. People could come to work, and everybody came to work. Many Serbs and many Croats did come, and many didn't. Those who failed to present for work were dismissed, and those who kept on coming to work stayed in the hospital until the very end, both Croats and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, during the siege of Vukovar, you had various dealings with the Defence staff of Vukovar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And a Crisis Staff was formed at Vukovar Hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Why was it considered necessary to create something called a Crisis Staff at the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the hospital was under threat. It faced a crisis. There were not enough medicines. We were short-staffed. It was constantly shelled. It was a target. That's why we set up a Crisis Staff. Its members were hospital employees, my assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you consider it necessary to liaise or coordinate with the defence staff of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because Vukovar was besieged. We could not evacuate the wounded. We could not receive medicines or medical supplies or even food.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in your dealings with the defence staff during the bombardment of Vukovar, the destruction of the city that was ongoing, was there ever any discussion about surrendering to the Serb forces August, September, October, November?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear that. I was not in communication with the defence staff within that context. When I went there, I would go to hand in our request for assistance for medical supplies and medicines. As for any military strategy, I never discussed those things with them. They did not discuss those things were me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was there any discussion amongst civilians or fighters or soldiers or people who you came in contact with that considering the extent of the damage and the numbers of individuals being killed it might be prudent to surrender?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not discuss that with me. What we did discuss was the help that we all hoped for. Just like we expected aid with medicines and medical supplies in the hospital, they expected help in manpower and weapons. On one occasion I spoke with Marin Vidic a day before the evacuation of the hospital, and he told me that he wanted to get in touch with Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: On the 18th of -- or I believe it was the 19th of October there was a convoy organised by Medecins sans Frontieres evacuating patients from the Vukovar Hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That convoy should have arrived on the 11th of October, but it did not reach any further than the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Doctor --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took all of the medicines and medical supplies from the lorries, and it was only on a second attempt on the 19th of October that the convoy did arrive at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did you hear that there was a problem in terms of the safe conduct of that passage to its final destination?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were supposed to arrive from the direction of Marinci, Bogdanovci, and Luzac. That was to be their route. And I heard that on the way back they hit an antitank mine and two nurses were injured on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did that occur because they were forced off of the route they were supposed to take?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, you talked in your testimony about Stipo Pole the chief of police in Vukovar. Do you know when and how he left Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I know, he left Vukovar on either the 17th or the 18th. I'm not sure. I saw him on the 17th. He was at the defence staff together with Marin Vidic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Does the name Tomo Jakovljevic mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tomo Jakovljevic was a paramedic in the Vukovar medical centre before the war. He worked in the plaster room.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was injured by a shell. He had a leg injury. And he was hospitalised as a patient in how -- in our hospital. And his leg was amputated. Like many other patients who had been treated and healed to a certain extent, he was transferred to other civilian shelters or to Borovo Komerc which was our reserve hospital with doctors and nurses. And all those whose health had improved to a certain extent ended up there. Tomo Jakovljevic was also sent there. Later I heard that he had actually been killed, but I don't know under what circumstances that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You never heard that he may have been murdered by Marko Mandic?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe that Marko Mandic was his colleague and friend. While he was still hospitalised, Marko Mandic visited him frequently and helped him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Who was Savo Damjanovic?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Savo Damjanovic was a medical technician, a paramedic, at the psychiatry ward. I remember his name. When I was first appointed the director of the medical centre in the month of July, I heard from Dr. Popovic that some people had taken him away from the hospital for interrogation. I called the police chief Stipe Pole to ask him whether he knew anything about that. He told me that he didn't know anything, and then I wrote an official request to the police asking them to investigate who had taken him away, whether it was possible to find that out, because I heard that some uniformed people had taken him away from his workplace in the hospital. This is all I know. I don't know anything else. I believe that the procedure is still underway, that the investigation is still underway, because many nurses went to the court to provide their affidavits. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was someone named Branko Kovacevic a doctor at the medical centre before the war?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 1D331, please. That's Defence tab 41.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is that bearded man in the centre of the photograph in the white suit, is that Branko Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know him as such. I remember him as an intern who worked before the war at the medical centre Vukovar, but at that time he didn't have a beard. But he was young. This man here is closer to middle age.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Didn't Mr. Kovacevic -- Dr. Kovacevic continue to work at the hospital until the middle of 1991?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an intern. I can't remember exactly where he worked, but when I became director of the medical centre, he was no longer working there. Perhaps he was among those who were not coming to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you can't recognise that -- that gentleman with the bothered as being the man whom you knew at the Vukovar Medical Centre?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Perhaps we could zoom in a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only say again I remember Branko Kovacevic the way he looked before 1991. I remember him and his fiancee, Olivera, who was also a doctor. I remember them, but I can't recognise him in this picture. Maybe it was taken much later. I can't tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did Dr. Kovacevic write poetry, as far as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 1D333, Defence tab 43, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this as a cover of a book?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we -- could we go to the next page, please. One moment, please. Could we have 1D334, please, which is Defence tab 44.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this as the cover of a book, Dr. Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. We can remove that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, do you remember when you first met Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there was one Dr. Hadzic, and I thought after asking about Dr. Kovacevic you were asking now about Dr. Hadzic. Goran Hadzic I met --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's a fair point, yes. I meant to ask you when did you first meet Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Goran Hadzic before the war as a patient's parent, because I was working in the paediatric ward treating his daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And over the years, how many times would you say that you treated his children?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly more. I only remember they came to see me for check-ups. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And would it accord with your recollection that he started to bring his children to you sometime around the middle of the 1980s and brought his children continuously to you up until May of 1991 for treatment?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, I don't remember exactly that whole period, but I remember they came to me for a check-up on the 2nd of May at the time of those events in Borovo Selo. I was seeing patients, and his wife and daughter were in my office at the outpatient clinic when I heard the news, and they said they had to leave immediately because something was going on in Borovo Selo. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you -- were you the only paediatrician at the Vukovar Hospital in the mid 1980s and the late 1980s and the early 1990s?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And were there --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let me just follow up with a question. Were there other paediatricians who were Serb?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other paediatricians, but I repeat to you as I said to the Court before, it didn't matter at all which patients and which doctors were Serb or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And that obviously was Mr. Hadzic's opinion as well, because he entrusted his children to your care; right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said before that it didn't matter at all, not then, not during the war, and not now. Patients were always treated as patients, not as members of an ethnic group. We didn't even ask about ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, I am sure you're aware that you have been the object of a number of inflammatory and I'm sure wholly unfounded allegations that you engaged in criminal conduct during the siege of Vukovar. Now, just to be clear to you, I'm not in any way suggesting that these allegations have foundation. I'm just asking you, do you know that those allegations exist?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've heard about it, of course. I've heard about it, and it was a problem for me, especially several years ago when I was supposed to make a statement to Serbian investigators regarding those allegations dating back to 1991. So of course I'm aware of it. However, they are unfounded accusations by people who said that Dr. Njavro and I did not treat all patients equally.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And do you think that the -- these allegations may have anything to do with the fact that you are a well-known figure on the Croat side upon whom you are an available target for false accusations?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I never analysed that. I don't know. I don't know who benefitted from make false statements about that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you know that at the end of 1992 or early 1993 Goran Hadzic appeared on a call-in programme in Belgrade on television, and one of the callers made allegations against you, and that Goran Hadzic publicly stated that he was sure that you had not committed these crimes? Are you aware that he did that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President. Dr. Bosanac, thank you very much for your answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gosnell. Redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I begin, may I ask whether there is at this stage any decision in relation to further examination on the issue of the notebooks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Two notebooks you want to add to your 65 ter list and ask Dr. Bosanac about the authenticity, whether she can --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: There were three of them, and we wished to ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And if memory serves, the Defence objects.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes. We e-mailed our response last night around 6.00, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you remind me the basis of your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The material is voluminous, it has not yet been fully translated, it has not been shown that there was due diligence in trying to obtain the material earlier, the underlying documentation in terms of a claimed RFA that was sent to the Serbian authorities has not been provided, no indication of an RFA to the Croatian authorities, and even assuming due diligence and good cause, given the extent of the material there's simply no way that we can deal with it in any way even if we limit the issue to authentication. We are simply not in a position to do that given the timing and the volume and the lack of translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this stage the motion is about adding these documents to the 65 ter list, and I understand it is a voluminous amount of material. However, again, in relation to the RFAs, we don't make it a habit to provide RFAs or any of our communications with States. However, if it could assist the Chamber in determining the issue, I do have the RFA in hard copy or can provide it on a confidential basis as well as the response we received. We did ask for the medical records of the hospital, the Vukovar Hospital, to the Serbian authorities, and we were told that they're not available. Again, if Your Honours wish to see them, we do have them. So at this stage if -- if you -- if your view is that this is too onerous on the Defence, we would seek to add them to the 65 ter list at this stage. However, as we've said in our motion, it would be a waste of resources to ask Dr. Bosanac to return to simply identify what these are, and I will not seek to ask any questions, any specific questions, about the entries or about the patients or any of that. I just would like her to look at them on the screen and tell everybody this is what she provided us and I will limit my questions to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And what you would produce on the screen, would that be that one page, if I'm right, that one page that you translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. We would display the cover -- the cover -- the first page of each notebook which has been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So your question -- your questions would be on the basis of that one page for each notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will allow the admission of the documents to the 65 ter exhibit list. It will allow the OTP to ask a few questions about authenticity and allow the Defence to cross Dr. Bosanac on this matter, and that will be as far as it goes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So at this stage I will strictly conduct a further re-examination, and I will wait for Mr. Gosnell's cross-examination before I re-examine on the questions he's put so far. Is that the way I should proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. And let me add to the ruling that your questions on these documents will only be based on the translated pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Much obliged.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: At the beginning of the proofing session on Saturday morning, is it correct to say that you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor a DVD? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And could you tell the Court what was contained in this DVD and how you came to obtain it?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know, for many years now we've in the Vukovar Hospital have been trying to get back the medical records that were taken away in 1991 to Belgrade. We have tried through the Foreign Ministry and through the Tribunal here in The Hague, but unfortunately we never managed to get back one single document from the Vukovar Hospital concerning year 1991. Two years ago these interstate negotiations were intensified, and two years ago in October the President of Serbia came to Vukovar to meet with the Croatian president, Josipovic, and I was invited to attend that meeting on behalf of many associations of detainees' and missing persons' families, and at that meeting I was told that part of the medical records had been returned. Those records and protocols were studied by the commission for detainees and missing persons for several months, and after that they sent them back to our hospital, and it was then that we established that those were documents from before the war, some case histories that had nothing to do with the war, and the only really important thing were the three notebooks kept by the head nurse of the hospital, including the list of all the wounded. That was very important to us then, and it's very important today, because now we have a record of all wounded persons for the period from July to November 1991, although these are not all the medical records. These are just lists in notebooks, which is a useful document, but it's not a proper medical record. Based on those documents we can now reconstruct precisely all the lists of persons who were wounded and who were in the hospital at that time and are still featuring on the lists of missing persons. And I believe it is important that before this Tribunal dealing with the Vukovar Hospital issues, all these documents should be available. I copied all these lists onto a DVD and handed them -- handed it over to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So, Doctor, do I understand it to be correct that these notebooks you provided on Saturday covered a period between July and November 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, these notebooks that you provided us on this DVD, from your answer do I gather that these were -- well, can you tell us who wrote -- who took down these -- these notes in the notebook?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head nurse of our hospital, Mrs. Vinazia [phoen] Kolesar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And what -- is this the only notebooks that were kept at the hospital recording the patients?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The patients were officially registered in protocols of urgent surgical admission, in surgery protocols and anaesthesiological protocols. Those are proper medical records. The notebooks we are talking about were useful to the head nurse and to us so that we could have at any point in time correct information on all the wounded persons who have been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when you say "all the wounded persons who have been admitted," can the Trial Chamber take these notebooks as a complete record of the wounded who were admitted at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the Chamber can, although these were not official documents. Those were documents that simply provided correct information. I suppose they're accurate and everything is written there, but the proper records are still in Belgrade and still have not been returned to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I will display the first notebook in a moment, but before I do that, can you tell the Trial Chamber what type of information they will find in those notebooks?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Name, last name of the wounded person, and the date of admission. This is very scant information, but it's important because it goes all the way up to the end. Before that we had information only up to 6 November.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May we display on the screen 65 ter 6408, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, do you recognise what we see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those are copies of this first notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And what is the date that we see at the top here? 4th of July 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Name and last name, Vlado Budimir; date of birth; address; and affiliation. We see here that he was a member of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And on this page we see for every entry or almost every entry what you call the affiliation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In the B/C/S version I would just like to, with your leave, Your Honours, go to page 91 to show the end date of this notebook. I know it's not page 1, but just to show the date wherever this notebook ends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You have translated that page?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: No, we haven't, but just to see the date. Although, I mean, we can ask the witness if she knows. Well, I mean, actually, it may not be necessary, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Should I ask the Defence position, or do you --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sure. Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: We don't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, this is almost the last page of this notebook. Do you see the date there?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We see it's the 25th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we move now to 65 ter 6409, please. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: This is the second notebook. Do you see the date of the 26th of September, 1991?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And do we see the same type of information as in the first notebook?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And if we scroll down in both B/C/S and English versions. Yes, that's fine. And can we now display -- oh, I notice the time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Mr. Demirdjian. Dr. Bosanac, it's time for our first break. We will come back at 11.00. You will be escorted out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we look for a moment to the timing. You plan to take -- how much time for your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, for re-examination I shouldn't be more than five or ten minutes depending on the answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So then I think it would be good to have the next witness available for the last session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That witness is in the waiting-room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. At this time, may I ask that we display on the screen 65 ter 6410, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, is this third notebook begin on the 25th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And does this notebook contain the same similar type of information compared to the first two notebooks we've seen so far?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And, Doctor, in relation to the information we find in these notebooks as you've explained to the Judges, generally we see the name, date of birth, and address, affiliation. Would it be correct that the affiliation is mentioned in relation to most of these patients?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As well as a diagnosis. I mean a medical diagnosis. That is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And just to be clear, these notebooks contain information relating to patients who are brought in to the hospital, and is that for any type of reason?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, is this about authenticity?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Just to complete as to what we find in the notebook itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I don't see any reaction from the Defence so proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I think that is my queue to object, Mr. President, and we've heard one or two questions already that have gone into the substance. I didn't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I do agree, Mr. Gosnell. I thought we -- the ruling was only about authenticity, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And, Doctor, in relation to these three notebooks, is it correct that they only indicate the date as to when the patient was received in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this stage I would propose to mark these three notebooks for identification pending fuller translations. That is for 65 ter 6408, 6409, and 6410.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The ruling was, Mr. Demirdjian, that we would allow you to admit them to the 65 ter list and that that would be all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So that's as far as we will go. We have now the witness's questions -- answers about authenticity, and now we'll wait what you will do, bar table motion or anything else, but for the moment we don't do anything more than admit them to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That concludes my further examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, cross-examination on this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: None, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Redirect, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, earlier yesterday counsel for the Defence asked you questions relating to the access to the hospital, the access to the hospital on the 19th of November, 1991. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: For the record --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: -- this is at page -- I'll repeat this is for page 3073 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you remember that in answering one of the questions of counsel you mentioned that one of the members of the White Eagles entered the hospital and he was the son of one of the doctors; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court who this doctor was?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could, but I can only do it in private session to exclude the general public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's okay. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And at page 4 of the transcript today and also yesterday, you were asked questions about the relationship between the paramilitaries and the JNA. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And today counsel asked you whether the paramilitaries were under the control of the JNA, and your answer was yes at that question; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, at the time in 1991, were you familiar with the military rules regulating the relationship between the TO and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Were you aware of any orders issued by the JNA relating to the relationship between the JNA and the TO at the time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Witness, during your testimony you have confirmed that one of your patients was a JNA soldier. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell me whether that JNA soldier was admitted before the fall of Vukovar, before Vukovar fell?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If that was indeed the case, could I then say that he hadn't been sent by his hierarchy but that he had arrived on his own or because he had been captured by the Croatian army and that the Croatian Army actually referred him to the hospital or brought him to the hospital? Would that be the case?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Members of the Croatian defence of Vukovar brought those soldiers in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After they were captured, obviously; right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know whether the authorities of the JNA knew that there were JNA troops hospitalised in your hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my appeals and in my telephone conversations I mentioned that before the fall of Vukovar. I told everybody that those soldiers were indeed in the hospital and that they were being treated there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now my last question: Do you understand why the JNA shelled and targeted the hospital? At least that's what you told us, that the JNA targeted and shelled the hospital. And why did they do that if their own soldiers were in the hospital? Do you have an explanation for that? Do you understand why that was going on?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never understood that, nor could I understand why they destroyed the entire town, why they were so angry after the fall of Vukovar. I could never understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, there is one issue I would like to clarify before we release the witness. It's your -- it's the OTP's answer to the issue on Monday in the transcript where we added the word "no" to an answer, and you seemed to have listened to the audio and heard the word "ni sam"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you for reminding me of this point. The word is "ne znam."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is "ne znam," so not "ni sam," which is different. Now, my reaction was, of course, not on what I heard in B/C/S but what I heard from the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And that was clearly "No." So that would be a translation problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Are you ready to deal with it or --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We will submit a request for verification of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So we don't have to bother the witness with this immediately for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam, Dr. Bosanac, we thank you for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal. You're now released as a witness, and we wish you a safe journey home. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we bring the next witness immediately? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The next witness is ready. May I be excused from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just before we begin, Your Honour, for the record, Prosecution's now represented by Matthew Gillett, analyst Sandra Rodriguez, and our intern Kai Leung, who has just entered the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, madam. Thank you for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal. First of all, do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us your name and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Visnja Bilic. I was born on the 20th of November, 1966.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You are about to read the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I need to point out to you that that declaration you are about to make does expose you to the penalty of perjury should you give false or untruthful or misleading information to the Tribunal. Can you now read the solemn declaration the usher will give you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gillett, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. At the outset you'll have noticed that there were four additional documents that the Prosecution will seek to use with this witness. These are documents 06406, 06407, 02498.1, and 06399. We've notified the Defence of our intention to use that, and as I understand, they've indicated no objection to that course of action. So we would seek to add them to the 65 ter list and have permission to use them with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is that correct as far as the Defence is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So these four documents are admitted to the 65 ter list, permitted to be added to the 65 ter list, and you may use them in your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. There was one additional document that's already on the 65 ter list and is already an admitted exhibit. It's admitted exhibit P1080, and we'd also seek to use that and we understand there's no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Defence's position is the same, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please proceed, Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Bilic. Is my voice coming through loud and clear?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: It is indeed. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could I ask you to state your profession and your current position?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: My current position is coordinator of the process for searching for missing persons and demonstration for detainees and missing persons. By profession I am a professor of psychology. I have a degree in psychology.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And could you state which -- which institution, sorry, you work for?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The administration for detainees and missing persons within the ministry for family, war veterans, and intergenerational solidarity of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And since when have you been involved with this institution in its various forms; that is, involved in this work, searching for missing persons and in relation to detained people?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Since 1993. For 20 years now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And have you testified before this Tribunal as an expert previously?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: I testified in two cases: in the Vojislav Seselj case and in the Stanisic-Simatovic case. I testified on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we get 65 ter document 03043 on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, do you recognise this as your curriculum vitae?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I'd seek for that to be admitted, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall Exhibit P1489, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I'm now going to ask you some questions about your expert report prepared for this case which is 65 ter document 05842, and I request if there's no objection to hand a hard copy of the report to Ms. Bilic along with one of the annexes that lists the victims, because there's a significant amount of data in these documents, and I'll be asking a number of questions about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, in your report you note that the administration for detained and missing persons, which I will call the administration from now on, keeps records on persons who were detained in enemy camps during the homeland war, also persons who went missing during the homeland war, and remains that were exhumed and identified during the homeland war. Can I ask you how frequently you deal with the records of missing persons in your daily work?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: In my daily work I handle files and missing persons data as well as the files on exhumations, on identified and non-identified mortal remains. This is part of my daily job.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Turning to the missing persons questionnaire forms, in your report at section 7 you state that the missing persons questionnaire form, the standard form used by your office, was created by an interdisciplinary team of professionals using the missing person forms of the ICRC, the UN centre for human rights, and Interpol as guides. Can I ask you did you personally participate in the creation of the questionnaire that your institution uses and if so how did you participate?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: I was personally involved in drafting this questionnaire, and in fact in one area which concerns the educational and family status of the missing person, I suggested some questions that became part of the questionnaire. Furthermore, I participated in so to speak standardising the questionnaire in order to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, could I ask you to lower the pace of your -- of what you are saying, because it's very difficult for the interpreters to follow if you speak that fast. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem. So I participated in creating a part of the questionnaire that concerns the educational and family status of the missing persons. I participated in the standardising of the questionnaire inasmuch as data is adapted to further digital processing of that information, and I was also involved in training the personnel who were involved in gathering data on missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: We see that on the form they record the data of disappearance of the missing person. Where does that information come from?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Information on the date of disappearance, just as all the other information in the questionnaire, came from the families of the missing persons who made applications for a search.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And for the people that are listed as missing with these forms, how do we know that they're still missing and that they haven't turned up alive since the time at which these missing persons questionnaires were filed?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The thing is that there are pretty strong recording mechanisms for keeping records on missing persons both internal and external. Among those mechanisms I can mention a continuous matching of the records of our Ministry of the Interior with the records of the Red Cross, also matching and comparison with the records of the ICRC and the international commission for missing persons. The fact is that records of missing persons have been made available to the relevant commissions in Serbia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and finally, they are publicly available to everyone, because they have also been published in the form of books but also on the web pages both of the ministry of defenders and the web sites of our Red Cross and the International Red Cross. So that list of missing persons in the Republic of Croatia is available to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: In your report you describe two actions. First there was an effort in 1994 to gather data regarding people who had gone missing during the war in Croatia up to that point, and then there was a second action in 2002 to 2006 which concerned primarily persons going missing during Operations Flash and Storm. Now, in your report at section 30, you refer to the figure of 984 missing persons tracing requests that are still open. Which action does that figure 984 refer to, the 1994 or the 2002 action?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The figure of 984 persons refers to the persons for whom data was collected in 1994. These persons in the majority of cases, over 95 per cent, went missing in 1991 and the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could I get 65 ter document 05845 on the monitor, please. And if we could go to page 8 of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, while this is come up, I note the slide that we're going is to see states that the large majority, 850 -- sorry, if we could get the next slide, please. Apologies. I believe this is the slide on page 7. I'll just check this. That's okay. I can simply cite the figure which is 853 out of 984 of the persons are listed as Croats. On what basis did you establish people's ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Information on the ethnicity of missing persons was obtained by the family members who made tracing requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And that's slide 5. Apologies, Your Honours. Now, if we now move to slide 7. This slide 7 shows that almost half of the people that are still missing disappeared from the county of Vukovar and Srem. And that's at the top of slide 7. Why are there still so many unsolved cases from this county?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
